title: Untangling Chip Traffic Jams
gist: As networks-on-chip stretch across chiplet boundaries, the hardest verification problems have migrated to the package edge, where coherency bugs surface as bring-up deadlocks months later and cost tape-out slips. Vendors from Cadence, Synopsys, Arteris, Axiomise, Vinci, Keysight and Baya Systems argue for shifting formal verification left of simulation (proving credit conservation, deadlock freedom and connectivity exhaustively), for whole-system multi-physics because thermally coupled dies invalidate per-die results, and for AI-fabric test focused on incast congestion and GPU idle time.

themes.theme: NoC boundary moves to the package edge

insights.claim: The speed gains from leading-edge AI accelerators and multi-die architectures can be lost entirely if on-chip networks are not optimized for the diverse data traffic moving between memories and processors.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Interconnect quality, not peak FLOPS, increasingly determines delivered AI performance — a reason spec-sheet comparisons of accelerators mislead.
insights.quote: The speed gains from leading-edge AI accelerators and multi-die architectures can be lost if on-chip networks are not optimized to handle diverse types of data traffic moving between memories and processors.

insights.claim: Networks-on-chip have evolved from simple on-chip layouts into a complex hierarchical orchestration layer that manages data flow across a heterogeneous system over its entire expected lifetime.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Reframes NoC IP from a routing utility to a lifetime system-management layer — supporting higher royalty capture for fabric IP vendors.

insights.claim: A NoC was originally designed to address wire congestion in layout, but its new challenge is facilitating across-die connection while ignoring the physical boundary — raising new questions about whether a multi-die system presents one network-on-chip or two with separate memory spaces.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: The unresolved single-versus-multiple-NoC question defines chiplet interoperability — a gating item for third-party chiplet marketplaces.
insights.quote: A network on chip was designed to address wire congestion layout, but its new challenge is how to facilitate that across-die connection, ignoring the physical connection

insights.claim: Arm wants its CPUs to sit next to Nvidia GPUs, and the mechanism being used is die-to-die interfaces built on AMBA CHI C2C, a cache-coherent chiplet-to-chiplet interface.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Names the concrete protocol underpinning Arm-plus-Nvidia packages — the standard to watch for who wins the coherent die-to-die interface layer.
insights.quote: For example, in the space of Nvidia GPUs, Arm wants to be the CPU next to it. How do you solve that? They’re looking at die-to-die interfaces utilizing AMBA CHI C2C (chiplet-to-chiplet), and that is a cache-coherent interface which solves their problem.

insights.claim: With chiplets, the NoC boundary has moved to the package edge, where timing, retry semantics and error handling are fundamentally different from on-die behavior that NoC architects already understand.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Explains why chiplet programs slip: the hardest interconnect problems have moved into a domain where existing design experience does not transfer.
insights.quote: The difficulty now is that with chiplets, the NoC boundary has moved to the package edge, where timing, retry semantics, and error handling are fundamentally different.

insights.claim: A coherent request reordered behind a non-coherent stream, or a credit returned on the wrong virtual channel, will not appear as a functional failure in simulation — it appears as a deadlock at bring-up months later, when the cost of finding it is enormous.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Quantifies the schedule risk in multi-die AI silicon: coherency bugs surface at bring-up, which is precisely when tape-out slips destroy product cycles.
insights.quote: A coherent request reordered behind a non-coherent stream, or a credit returned on the wrong virtual channel, is not going to show up as a functional failure in simulation

insights.claim: Cache coherency is harder to implement and heavier to verify than I/O coherency because it produces many more issues that are hard to find, and defining all the test cases is completely non-trivial.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Sets the difficulty ranking that determines verification cost and schedule for any coherent chiplet design — a hidden cost in the chiplet business case.
insights.quote: Defining all the cases is completely non-trivial. You must be really careful about how you build the environment around that.

insights.claim: Coherency test creation is shifting left via automatic test generation from constraints — describing intent such as writing to memory, moving it, then accessing it from software on a second core — rather than having users hand-write test cases; the approach is similar in spirit to Portable Stimulus but is not based on the PSS standard.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: A proprietary alternative to a ratified standard signals fragmentation in system-level verification methodology — watch whether PSS or vendor flows win.
insights.quote: This system for integrating different processors and automatically generating tests based on constraints is roughly in the same vein as Portable Stimulus, although it’s not based on the PSS standard and focuses on cache coherency.

insights.claim: The more AI compute packed into a device, the more the I/O perimeter must be treated as a first-class system resource, with bandwidth density, latency determinism, congestion control, quality of service and error containment becoming architectural constraints rather than post-layout problems.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Elevates fabric and I/O architecture to an early design decision — the structural argument for commercial NoC IP vendors like Arteris capturing more of the design.
insights.quote: Bandwidth density, latency determinism, congestion control, quality of service, and error containment become architectural constraints, not post-layout problems
insights.locator: Andy Nightingale, Arteris — 'AI forces I/O considerations'

insights.claim: Interconnects are not difficult designs but they are big, and the number of lines is off the charts, with companies now issuing directives that every line has to be simulated.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: A pure compute-demand signal: exhaustive line-level interconnect simulation drives EDA license and cloud compute consumption independent of node migration.
insights.quote: What we’re seeing is capacity, capacity, capacity. People want to simulate the entire interconnect of chiplets to study as many lines as possible, if not all.

insights.claim: A system of multiple dies and chiplets has superimposed, spatially distributed power maps that thermally couple, so the global hotspot may not coincide with any single chip's local maximum and independent single-chip thermal results cannot simply be added up.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Invalidates per-die thermal sign-off for multi-die packages — a methodology gap that shows up as field failures or forced power derating in AI systems.
insights.quote: Thermal activity in one chip raises its neighbors’ baseline, and the global hotspot may not coincide with any single chip’s local maximum. You cannot simply add up independent single-chip results.

insights.claim: The number of system-level scenarios that matter — across power states, stack configurations and boundary conditions — makes sequential, specialist-run solves impractical as a design workflow, requiring a fundamentally different throughput model for physics simulation.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: The argument for GPU-accelerated or continuously running physics solvers as a new EDA category — a spending shift from accuracy to throughput.
insights.quote: The number of scenarios that matter at the system level — across different power states, stack configurations, and boundary conditions — makes sequential, specialist-run solves impractical as a design workflow

insights.claim: Transient thermal loading in multi-die systems drives warpage, low-K dielectric cracking and delamination, and can turn latent defects into real defects, so no single node can be isolated and expected to hold.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Mechanical failure modes are now first-order reliability risks in advanced packages — a yield and warranty exposure for AI accelerator vendors.
insights.quote: Warpage, low-K dielectric cracking, and delamination are also concerns driven by the system’s transient thermal loading.
insights.locator: Satish Radhakrishnan, Vinci — 'Simulating NoCs is a multi-physics challenge'

insights.claim: Advanced packaging choices — Intel's EMIB, TSMC's CoWoS, and hybrid bonding — impose real constraints on bump pitch, redistribution and thermal envelope, and the choice between 2.5D and 3D affects floorplan and power delivery network, so packaging can no longer be handed off downstream.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Packaging technology selection now constrains front-end design, meaning capacity allocation at TSMC/Intel packaging effectively locks a design's architecture early.
insights.quote: Teams used to treat packaging as something you handed off downstream. That doesn’t work anymore.
insights.locator: Ashish Darbari, Axiomise — 'Advanced packaging options also bring challenges'

themes.theme: Formal verification as the NoC safety net

insights.claim: Cross-protocol corner cases such as UCIe link states combined with CHI snoop transactions combined with NoC arbitration cannot be simulated through, but formal verification can prove credit conservation, deadlock freedom, ordering properties and protocol compliance at every interface.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: The technical case for formal tools moving from niche to mandatory in chiplet designs — a growth vector for formal verification vendors.
insights.quote: For example, UCIe link states, combined with CHI snoop transactions, combined with NoC arbitration is not something you can simulate your way through

insights.claim: By the time a multi-die system reaches emulation, a coherence or deadlock bug costs a tape-out slip, which is why formal is being shifted left of simulation.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Links verification methodology directly to tape-out schedule risk — the ROI argument that gets formal budget approved at chiplet-era design houses.
insights.quote: By the time a multi-die system is in emulation, a coherence or deadlock bug costs you a tape-out slip.

insights.claim: Formal verification can prove structural connectivity and reachability for every legal source-destination pair in a mesh, torus or custom topology rather than sampling selected routes in simulation, with symmetry-based reduction and induction on hop count making the proofs scale beyond toy topologies.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that exhaustive NoC proofs are now practical at scale — removing a long-standing objection to formal adoption in interconnect.
insights.quote: Symmetry-based reduction and induction on hop count are the practical techniques that make these proofs scale beyond toy topologies.

insights.claim: Credit-based flow control can be verified by proving that in-flight flits targeting a downstream buffer never exceed the credit budget or FIFO depth, with credits returned exactly when storage is freed — never early, never lost, never double-counted — because misaligned credit accounting is a common source of latent NoC bugs.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Identifies the single most common latent NoC defect class, which is where verification spend and tool differentiation will concentrate.
insights.quote: misalignment in credit accounting is a common source of latent NoC bugs

insights.claim: Fault scenarios such as a dead router, stuck link or buffer error can be modeled as non-deterministic fault injections in formal, which naturally explores all placements and timings of the fault within scope.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Formal fault injection is the credible path to safety certification for AI and automotive fabrics — relevant to ISO 26262-class qualification cost.
insights.quote: Formal is great for fault modeling, as inherently it runs unconstrained and the non-determinism comes naturally to formal

insights.claim: SystemC and transaction-level models are useful for early architectural exploration, but RTL-level formal verification is required to prove cycle-accurate properties like exact credit behavior, arbitration delays and clock-domain-crossing safety, because many real NoC bugs come from single-cycle races invisible in transaction-level models.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: A balanced-methodology prescription that implies design teams must buy both architectural and formal tools — expanding total verification spend per design.
insights.quote: many real NoC bugs arise from single-cycle races and implementation details that are invisible in transaction-level models

themes.theme: Testing AI fabrics and incast congestion

insights.claim: Testing AI fabrics now includes fine-tuning the fabric to minimize GPU idle times and observing the impact of scaling traffic to hundreds of ports on the fabric and protocol deployment.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: GPU idle time is the economic metric of an AI cluster — fabric test equipment sells directly against dollars of stranded accelerator capex.
insights.quote: This includes assessing and fine-tuning your AI fabric to ensure that you’re minimizing GPU idle times
insights.locator: Razvan Arhip, Keysight Technologies — 'Testing and emulating NoCs'

insights.claim: A defining difference between pre-AI and AI-era traffic is the frequency of incast network bottlenecks, which occur during many-to-one communication when GPUs exchange traffic in all-to-all or reduce-ring patterns after computing on data.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Incast congestion is the specific failure mode AI networking gear must solve — the technical basis for premium pricing on congestion-aware switches and NICs.
insights.quote: There’s a lot of incast inside the AI fabric in data centers, because after the GPUs take the data and perform operations on the data, they exchange traffic in various patterns, such as all-to-all, or reduce ring, and so on

insights.claim: Realistic AI fabric emulation deliberately avoids perfect synchronization between endpoints, randomizing timing because nanosecond-level synchronization does not exist in the real world.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Test realism determines whether congestion-control claims survive deployment — a reason vendor lab benchmarks overstate real cluster performance.
insights.quote: But we do not perfectly synchronize it, because there’s no such thing in the real world.

insights.claim: Impairment testing at the data plane — delaying, losing or dropping packets and adding jitter in various patterns — is a vital part of validating how AI fabric protocols behave.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Impairment test capability is a differentiator in network test equipment as AI fabrics push protocols like RoCEv2 to their limits.
insights.quote: We can delay, lose, or drop packets

insights.claim: Large AI data center operators anticipate that chips will eventually wear out over time, but automotive designs cannot tolerate that, so automotive NoCs require extra bits on every data path for error detection, immediate control-plane notification, and in some cases redundant logic running in parallel with nanosecond-level recovery.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Explains the hard cost and area premium of automotive-grade fabric IP, and why data-center silicon cannot simply be re-badged for vehicles.
insights.quote: With a lot of the big data centers that are doing AI, they anticipate that eventually, over time, chips are going to wear out. But you can’t have that in your car.
insights.locator: Kent Orthner, Baya Systems — 'NoC reliability: data center vs. auto'

insights.claim: Automotive data flows resemble data center flows in kind if not in scale, and the inference engines running in cars will become common as self-driving and driver-assist features spread — with safety, not throughput, front and center.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Automotive becomes a second high-volume market for AI fabric and inference IP, but qualified at a different price and certification bar.
insights.quote: It’s just that safety now becomes front and center.

insights.claim: AI training and inference are only as fast as the networks transporting data between dedicated processors and memory, just as a software-defined vehicle is only as reliable as the networks supporting communication across its zonal architecture.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: The single-sentence framing for why interconnect IP and network test are structural beneficiaries of both the AI and SDV transitions.
insights.quote: AI training and inference are only as fast as the networks transporting the data between dedicated processors and memory.
